about: The editable standard examples and the failure examples, as model records of schema version 1 (src/record.js). Each variable, equation, condition and assumption has a stable id. Values are illustrative inputs for the example, not measured data.

examples.label: Convection: Pi groups
examples.title: Convective heat transfer: the worked Buckingham Pi calculation

purpose.question: On which independent dimensionless groups does the heat-transfer coefficient of a body in a flow depend?

geometry.domain: A body of characteristic length L in a uniform flow of speed U
geometry.coordinates: None, because the calculation uses the Pi variables only
geometry.interfaces: The body surface

assumptions.text: All reference quantities are positive.
The inputs have no additional constraints.
k is the conductivity of the fluid, so hL/k is a Nusselt number and not a Biot number.

evidence.claim: The worked calculation gives rank 4 and the groups hL/k, μ/(ρUL) and ρc_pUL/k for the repeating variables ρ, U, L, k.

examples.title: Straight fin with an insulated tip: the complete Pi basis

variables.meaning: Heat flow at the fin base

geometry.domain: A straight fin of length L, constant cross-section A_c and exposed perimeter P
geometry.coordinates: x along the fin, from the base (x = 0) to the tip (x = L)
geometry.interfaces: The base at x = 0 and the insulated tip at x = L

assumptions.text: The conductivity is constant.
The surface convection is uniform.
The tip is insulated.
ΔT = T_b − T_∞ is not 0.
Temperature varies along x only. The transverse-conduction validity condition needs a separate derivation.

evidence.claim: The time row equals −3 times the mass row, the rank is 3 and the variable set has 4 independent groups.
m²L² = hPL²/(kA) is the fin parameter of the insulated-tip solution.

Kinematic viscosity of the model fluid
Thermal diffusivity of the model fluid
Temperature drop across the layer, T_h − T_c
Horizontal distance from the left wall

equations.text: d(omega,t) + d(psi,z)*d(omega,x) - d(psi,x)*d(omega,z) = nu*(d(omega,x,x) + d(omega,z,z)) - g*beta*d(T,x)

geometry.domain: A two-dimensional cell of depth H and width L = H between horizontal plates. The cell holds one roll of a periodic layer of period 2H
geometry.coordinates: x from the left wall (x = 0) to the right wall (x = L). z from the lower plate (z = 0) to the upper plate (z = H). Time t
geometry.interfaces: No-slip isothermal plates at z = 0 and z = H. Stress-free adiabatic side walls at x = 0 and x = L

assumptions.text: The Boussinesq approximation applies: βΔT = 8/300 ≪ 1, and the properties are constant.
The flow is two-dimensional. With stress-free adiabatic side walls, the box holds exactly the mirror-symmetric rolls of a periodic layer of period 2L.
A model fluid with ν = κ, so Pr = 1, the value of Wen, Goluskin and Doering (2022).
T_h is above T_c.

scales.reason: The depth is the length scale of both coordinates, so the cell is 0 < X < Γ, 0 < Z < 1.
The depth is the length scale.
The time that heat takes to diffuse across the layer.
The thermal diffusion velocity κ/H times the depth H.
The stream function scale over H².
θ = (T − T_c)/ΔT decreases from 1 at the lower plate to 0 at the upper plate.

evidence.claim: Steady rolls between no-slip plates at Pr = 1: onset near Ra_c ≈ 1708 and Nu of rolls of period 2 (Table 1S).

examples.label: Lumped body with radiation

variables.meaning: Emissivity of the oxidized surface (an assumed value)
Volume: a cube of side 1 cm
Specific heat capacity of pure copper

geometry.domain: A copper cube with a side of 1 cm, small compared with the chamber
geometry.coordinates: Time t only
geometry.interfaces: The cube's surface, in radiative exchange with the chamber walls at T_e

assumptions.text: The temperature of the cube is uniform: the radiation Biot number is far below 0.1.
The surface is grey and diffuse, and the chamber is large and at a uniform temperature.
There is no convection: the chamber holds a vacuum.
The properties of copper are constant at their 20 °C values (Table A.1). The dimensional time constant uses these values.

scales.reason: Radiation needs absolute temperatures, so θ = T/T_e with the chamber temperature as the reference.
The radiative time scale: heat capacity over εσA_sT_e³.

evidence.claim: Pure copper: ρ = 8954 kg/m³, c_p = 384 J/(kg·K), k = 398 W/(m·K) (Table A.1).
σ = 5.670374419…×10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, exact in the SI.

examples.label: Surface radiation
examples.title: Radiation in a long duct: crossed-string view factors, reciprocity and the radiosity network

purpose.question: How much heat does a hot floor radiate to a cold ceiling across a long duct, when the side walls reradiate all that they absorb?

variables.meaning: Net radiative heat flux of the floor
View factor from the floor to the ceiling
View factor from the floor to the side walls

geometry.domain: A long duct of width W = 4 and height H = 3 (in any one length unit): floor, ceiling and two side walls
geometry.coordinates: None: the radiosity network has no coordinate
geometry.interfaces: Four grey diffuse surfaces

assumptions.text: The floor is not black: ε₁ < 1.
The ceiling is not black: ε₂ < 1.
Grey diffuse surfaces with a uniform temperature and radiosity on each.

The side walls are adiabatic, so they reradiate all that they absorb. Floor and ceiling have the same width. Thus each side wall sees the floor and the ceiling with the same view factor, and this view factor divides out of the side-wall balance.

scales.reason: The emissive power of the floor scales every radiosity.
The same scale for every radiosity.
The same scale for every radiosity.

evidence.claim: Radiosity networks of grey surfaces, view factor reciprocity and summation, and the string rule for two-dimensional view factors.

examples.title: Laminar flow between parallel plates with a uniform heat flux at both walls

purpose.question: Which pressure gradient drives a given mean velocity between two parallel plates, and which heat-transfer coefficient does a uniform heat flux at both walls give?

variables.meaning: Local temperature minus the wall temperature, T − T_w
Half of the gap between the plates
Heat flux into the air at each wall
Pressure gradient that drives the flow, −dp/dx
Rise of the bulk temperature along the channel, dT_m/dx

geometry.domain: Two wide parallel plates at y = −b and y = b, far from the inlet; by symmetry the model uses the half 0 ≤ y ≤ b
geometry.coordinates: y from the centre plane (y = 0) to the wall (y = b); x along the flow
geometry.interfaces: The walls at y = ±b

assumptions.text: The flow is steady, laminar and fully developed between wide plates.
The fluid is Newtonian with constant properties.
Both walls receive the same uniform heat flux, and the temperature profile is fully developed. Viscous heating is small.

scales.reason: The half-gap is the length scale, so Y = y/b runs from 0 at the centre plane to 1 at the wall.
The mean velocity is the velocity scale.
The wall heat flux sets the temperature difference across the half-gap.

evidence.claim: Plane Poiseuille flow has a parabolic profile and f·Re = 96 with the hydraulic diameter 4b.

examples.label: Nozzle flow
examples.title: Air in a converging-diverging nozzle: sonic throat and choked mass flow

purpose.question: Which mass flow passes through a converging-diverging nozzle from a reservoir of air, and when is the throat sonic?

variables.meaning: Specific heat capacity of air at constant pressure
Cross-section area at the station considered

geometry.domain: A converging-diverging nozzle between a large reservoir and a space at the back pressure; the area falls from A_i to A_t at the throat and rises to A_e at the exit
geometry.coordinates: x along the axis; the area A(x) is given
geometry.interfaces: The throat and the exit plane

assumptions.text: Quasi-one-dimensional steady flow: the properties are uniform over each cross-section.
Air is an ideal gas with constant specific heats, γ = 7/5 and c_p = 7R_g/2.
The flow is adiabatic, has no friction and no shock: it is isentropic.

scales.reason: The stagnation density ρ₀ = p₀/(R_gT₀).
The speed √(R_gT₀) of the reservoir state.
The stagnation temperature.
The stagnation pressure.

evidence.claim: The mass flow is largest when the throat is sonic, M = 1; it then depends on p₀, T₀ and A_t only.

examples.label: Hydraulic jump
examples.title: Shallow water in a wide flat channel: supercritical inflow and its hydraulic jump

purpose.question: Which downstream depth makes a hydraulic jump form in a fast, shallow flow, and how much energy does the jump take from the flow?

geometry.domain: A wide rectangular channel with a flat, horizontal bed; the water covers the whole reach
geometry.coordinates: x along the channel from the inflow (x = 0) to the outflow (x = L)
geometry.interfaces: The free surface

assumptions.text: Long waves on a thin layer: the pressure is hydrostatic and the velocity is uniform over the depth.
The bed is flat and horizontal and has no friction. The water covers the whole reach.
A jump keeps mass and momentum and loses energy.

scales.reason: The length of the reach.
The depth of the inflow.
The velocity of the inflow.

evidence.claim: The conjugate depth ratio h₂/h₁ = (√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1)/2 and the head loss (h₂ − h₁)³/(4h₁h₂).

examples.label: Flat-plate boundary layer
examples.title: Laminar boundary layer on a flat plate (Blasius)

purpose.question: Which wall shear stress and which layer thickness does a uniform stream of air give on a flat plate, and where is the boundary-layer approximation accurate?

variables.meaning: Distance of the station from the leading edge
Outer edge of the computation, far outside the layer
Wall shear stress at the station

geometry.domain: A thin flat plate parallel to a uniform stream, with a sharp leading edge
geometry.coordinates: x along the plate from the leading edge; y normal to the plate
geometry.interfaces: The plate surface y = 0

assumptions.text: Steady, laminar, two-dimensional flow of a fluid with constant properties.
The outer stream is uniform, so the pressure along the plate is constant.
The layer is thin: Re_L = UL/ν is large, and y_e is far outside the layer.

scales.reason: The distance of the station from the leading edge.
The inner scale: the thickness at which viscosity balances inertia.
The outer speed.
The inner scale of v: continuity with the inner thickness.

evidence.claim: The Blasius solution gives f''(0) = 0.332 and c_f = 0.664/√Re_x.

examples.label: Airfoil in potential flow
examples.title: A cambered Joukowski airfoil in a uniform stream: surface pressure, lift and thin-airfoil theory

purpose.question: Which lift does a thin cambered airfoil give at a small angle of attack, and where is thin-airfoil theory accurate?

variables.meaning: Camber ratio: largest camber over the chord
Thickness parameter of the Joukowski circle

geometry.domain: The plane outside a Joukowski airfoil of chord c; the far-field boundary is a square of half-width X_f. The airfoil surface and its sharp trailing edge are part of the declared solver (a conformal map), because a curved surface is not a condition at x = constant
geometry.coordinates: x along the stream, y normal to it; the chord makes the angle α with the stream
geometry.interfaces: The airfoil surface

assumptions.text: Incompressible, inviscid flow without vorticity outside the airfoil, at high Reynolds number with attached flow.
No flow through the airfoil surface, and the Kutta condition: the flow leaves the sharp trailing edge smoothly.
The far-field boundary is far from the airfoil: X_f ≫ c.

scales.reason: The chord.
The chord.
The stream speed times the chord.

evidence.claim: Thin-airfoil theory gives c_l = 2π(α − α_L0).
